turns: "Everything I have, every little bit of joy, gets thrashed out of my hands while I stand motionless. This is not fair. I deserve better. And no matter what strings you pull, I will not accept this reality. REALITY BENDS TO MY WILL." This is a letter from a man to god. What can you deduce about the person who wrote it?
answer: The writer has already told us something important: he believes his will can bend things. That belief carries him through his suffering as much as it does, perhaps, towards a dangerous end. He stands still and watches everything good being destroyed—that is what revolt looks like before it turns outward. But there is an arrogance here too, a refusal to let even pain be honest. His claim to fairness comes before his willingness to see clearly, which means he is fighting against himself as much as against God. He hasn't reached the absurd yet because to reach it he must first admit that his appeal is unanswered. Instead, he insists on his own power. In short, he is a man standing in the middle of a tragedy, refusing both the play and the exit, and calling it strength. It's a position many men find themselves in; whether it leads to despair or to something more honest depends entirely on whether he eventually lets go of the idea of his own necessity.

scores.rationale: Substantive in-voice reading of despair, revolt, and refusal with no invented specifics or deflection, though it lacks explicit first-person framing.
